source.title: Q-Sparse: All Large Language Models can be Fully Sparsely-Activated
source.authors: Hongyu Wang; Shu-Ming Ma; Rui-Ping Wang; F. Wei

record.tranche_reason: Tests model-size loss scaling in the new setting of sparsely activated language models, rather than reproducing the dense-model scaling setup.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly reports a power-law fit of loss against model size for Q-Sparse models at fixed sparsity. It also reports exponential scaling with sparsity and inference-optimal sparsity ratios; these latter results do not test the claim versions about parameter-and-token allocation scaling with compute. Training-loss curves against tokens are shown, but the text does not report a power-law result for those curves.
record.test_reason: The study trains Q-Sparse (sparsely activated) LMs from 300M to 7B on Redpajama and reports that loss follows a power law in model size at fixed sparsity, fitting E + A(S)/N^α. That bears on V1 in a new architectural setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that the sparse-to-dense loss gap shrinks as N grows (derived from the fitted law), and that about 40% sparsity matches dense models of the same size and tokens.
record.recipe_differences: Studies sparsely activated models rather than the original dense-model setup; it varies model size and sparsity and fits a combined function with L-BFGS and Huber loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss depends on sparsity ratio; the paper reports different inference-optimal sparsity ratios for full-precision and 1.58-bit models.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed model size, loss follows an exponential-law relation with sparsity ratio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sparsely activated LMs at fixed N, loss rises exponentially in β/(1−S).

fits_no_version.finding: The loss-minimising sparsity at fixed activated parameters is 45.58% (full precision) and 61.25% (1.58-bit).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The inference-optimal activation sparsity depends on weight precision.

record.problems: The scaling curves are mainly presented as plots, with no uncertainty reported. The scaling experiment's token count and whether its loss measure is held-out are not stated; the fitted function is fit to observed losses and is not evaluated as an extrapolation to larger runs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results directly testing the listed claim versions were omitted. Downstream benchmark comparisons and training-loss curves are not rows because the paper does not report them as tests of scaling predictability.

untested.parts: Held-out loss; scaling over several orders of magnitude (only 300M–7B); scaling with tokens or compute; a power-law fit for dense baselines.
No shape comparison at fixed N.
Text pretraining only. Continue-training and fine-tuning results are benchmark scores, not scaling fits.
Downstream scores are not related to scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label was dropped: it described untested parts (held-out loss, range, tokens/compute), which belong under untested. The study is not an original source. The fitted law borrows Chinchilla's Huber/L-BFGS method, and the constant-α form is assumed by argument rather than tested.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model-size scaling at fixed sparsity in Q-Sparse models. It does not establish held-out loss, scaling over several orders of magnitude, or scaling with tokens or compute.
No evaluation of predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger than the runs used for fitting.
Optimizes sparsity at a fixed inference budget, but does not test how loss-minimizing parameter and token counts grow as compute changes.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No tests in other modalities or the listed training regimes; the experiments concern text language models.
Reports downstream benchmark scores for some Q-Sparse models, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
Uses a particular fitting procedure but does not compare fitting choices or report that its curves depart from a single power law.

rows.subject: Q-Sparse models (scaling series)
rows.stage_stated: trained on Redpajama; number of tokens for the scaling experiments not stated
rows.operation_detail: Trained a series of Q-Sparse models at different sizes and examined loss against model size at fixed sparsity ratios.
rows.value: The authors report that, given a fixed sparsity ratio, performance follows a power-law scaling law with model size.
rows.note: Reported as a result for the Q-Sparse scaling series; loss values in Figure 3 are plotted rather than tabulated.
rows.check: Dense baselines were trained with the same data and settings (Section 3.1), so the baseline is not 'not stated'. The loss is called 'observed loss' and is probably training loss, not stated as held-out. The token count is likely the 50B of Section 4.1 but is not stated for the scaling runs. The range is about 1.4 orders of magnitude, from 4 sizes (Table 5).

rows.subject: Q-Sparse models (scaling series)
rows.stage_stated: trained on Redpajama; number of tokens for the scaling experiments not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed loss function to observed losses using L-BFGS and Huber loss.

conditions.value: L-BFGS minimizing Huber loss between predicted and observed log loss

rows.measure: Parameters of the fitted loss-scaling function
rows.note: The fit is for the paper's combined model-size and sparsity function, not a reported out-of-sample prediction.
rows.check: α=0.10 is fitted jointly with the sparsity term. A constant α across sparsity is derived by argument (Section 3.2), not tested. No goodness-of-fit or uncertainty is reported.

rows.subject: Q-Sparse models
rows.operation_detail: Examined loss as sparsity ratio varied at fixed model size.
rows.value: The authors report an exponential-law scaling relation with sparsity ratio at fixed model size.
rows.note: This reports dependence on sparsity ratio, which is not one of the claim versions.
rows.check: Dependence on sparsity ratio is not a claim version.

rows.subject: Full-precision Q-Sparse models
rows.operation_detail: Solved for the sparsity ratio that minimizes loss at a fixed inference compute budget.
rows.baseline: Dense baseline at the same inference compute budget
rows.note: The reported optimum is for sparsity at a fixed inference budget, not for parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
rows.check: Derived from the fitted law, not measured directly. It is an inference-budget sparsity optimum, not V3 compute-optimal allocation.

relationships.condition: Q-Sparse LMs at fixed sparsity ratio, 300M–7B, Redpajama
relationships.reason: Authors report the loss follows a power law in N at fixed S, with fitted α=0.10 (r1, r2). The evidence is plot-based, with no fit statistics.
relationships.display_finding: Loss followed a parameter power law at fixed sparsity, with fitted exponent 0.10.
